content: Dr. John Edward McGinness, who held both a PhD in Physics and an MD, was a pioneering figure in the fields of organic electronics and nanotechnology. He earned his Bachelor of Science in Physics from the University of Houston in 1966, followed by a PhD in Physics from Rice University in 1970. Later, he obtained his MD from the University of Texas Medical School at Houston in 1985. Over the course of his career, Dr. McGinness authored approximately 40 research publications, book chapters, and presentations. In 1972, while working in the Metallurgy Department at Youngstown State University, Dr. McGinness proposed that electronic conduction in melanins (such as polyacetylene, polypyrrole, and polyaniline blacks) was analogous to conduction in amorphous solids like chalcogenide glasses. This concept, originally explored by Neville Mott and others, involved mechanisms such as mobility gaps, phonon-assisted hopping, polarons, and quantum tunneling. His work anticipated the Nobel Prize-winning research of Shirakawa and colleagues on conduction mechanisms in oxidized polyacetylenes. Dr. McGinness later joined the Physics Department at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, where he explored the physical properties of melanin as a potential avenue for treating melanoma. At the time, this was a relatively obscure area of research, with few researchers outside of melanoma studies investigating the electronic properties of rigid-backbone polymer blacks. Notably, Bolto and colleagues had previously reported high conductivity in iodine-doped polypyrrole, but this remained a niche interest. Inspired by the switching behavior observed in chalcogenide glasses, where a material transitions between low-conductivity (OFF) and high-conductivity (ON) states under a threshold voltage, Dr. McGinness hypothesized that melanins might exhibit similar voltage-controlled switching. He and his colleagues at MD Anderson constructed a voltage-controlled switch using melanin as the active element, demonstrating its electronic behavior and validating his model for conduction in such materials. This device served as a proof of concept and directly anticipated the work that led to the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery and development of conductive polymers. Dr. McGinness' device was groundbreaking in several ways. It was the first identifiable active organic semiconductor device, meaning it used current or voltage to control current flow. This innovation laid the foundation for many subsequent developments in organic electronics. Furthermore, the device is considered the first nanotechnology device, as organic electronics are a subset of nanotechnology. The Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History now houses this device as part of its collection of early electronic devices. The device also demonstrated a high-conductivity ON state with metallic-like properties in linear-backbone conductive polymers, a significant advancement at the time. A subsequent article in Nature highlighted the material's strikingly large conductivity and high conductivity. Today, oxidized polyacetylenes and their derivatives are among the most widely used commercial conductive polymers. Additionally, the device exhibited negative differential resistance, a property now well-recognized in electronically active conductive polymers. Dr. McGinness' contributions to organic electronics were not fully appreciated until decades later. A 2003 review of molecular electronics noted that his 1974 work with Corry and Proctor represented the first experimental demonstration of an operating molecular electronic device. This device functioned in line with biopolymer conduction theories proposed by Szent-Györgyi and exhibited strong negative differential resistance, a hallmark of modern molecular electronics. Beyond organic electronics, Dr. McGinness conducted significant research on the role of free radicals in the action and toxicity of anticancer drugs such as cisplatin, adriamycin, and bleomycin. He was the first to demonstrate that cisplatin-induced kidney toxicity involves reactive oxygen species. Some of this work was conducted with Dr. Harry Demopoulos, who was known for his involvement in the Doris Duke will dispute and his role as a medical consultant in Clint Eastwood's Dirty Harry films. Dr. McGinness also explored dielectric spectroscopy of water bound to membranes, a line of research that contributed to the development of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Additionally, he and his colleagues obtained two U.S. patents for organic-polymer-based energy storage devices (batteries), specifically U.S. Patents 4,366,216 and 4,504,557. Dr. McGinness' extensive body of work includes numerous publications, such as his seminal 1972 paper in Science on mobility gaps in melanins and his 1974 paper on amorphous semiconductor switching in melanins. His research spanned topics such as the thermal and electronic properties of melanins, the dielectric interactions of melanin-water-ion systems, and the mechanisms of drug-induced toxicity. His contributions to both organic electronics and medical research have left a lasting impact on their respective fields.
